South Korea Imposes New Tariffs on Shipping Equipment Imports, Disrupting Transportation & Logistics Firms

SEOUL, June 13—South Korea’s Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy has imposed a new round of tariffs on imported transportation and logistics equipment, sending shockwaves through the nation’s shipping and freight sector, industry sources said Thursday.

The tariffs, which took effect earlier this week, apply to a range of products including container handling machinery, port vehicles, and other specialized logistics equipment. The measure is widely viewed as a response to what officials have called “unfair trade practices” by foreign manufacturers, although the ministry did not specify any single country or company as the target.

“South Korea must act to protect its domestic logistics sector and ensure a level playing field for local manufacturers,” said Deputy Trade Minister Kim Hyun-soo at a press briefing. “The new tariffs are a temporary but necessary measure as we continue negotiations with our trade partners.”

The move has drawn immediate concern from major players in the shipping industry, who warn that the tariffs are already driving up costs and delaying key upgrades to critical infrastructure. Pan Ocean Co Ltd, one of South Korea’s largest bulk shipping operators, said in a statement that the tariffs would have “an adverse impact on the timely modernization of our logistics assets.” The company added that it is reviewing procurement plans and seeking alternative suppliers, but warned that supply chain disruptions are possible in the coming weeks.

Park Jae-min, an analyst at the Korea Shipping Research Institute, said the tariffs could increase logistics costs by as much as 12 percent for some operators. “Many companies, especially those relying on advanced imported equipment, are now facing difficult choices,” Park noted. “There is a risk that project timelines for port expansion and fleet renewal will slip.”

The Korea Transportation & Logistics Association also expressed concern, stating, “The industry is already under pressure from rising fuel costs and global supply chain volatility. Additional tariffs on essential equipment could undermine competitiveness.”

As of Thursday, some shipments of foreign-made cranes and container trucks destined for Busan and Incheon ports were reportedly held at customs pending tariff assessments, according to local shipping agents. The government said it will monitor the effects of the tariffs and consider adjustments if necessary, but gave no indication of when the measure might be lifted.
